forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Broxtowe's 2025/26 General Fund underspent by £2.5m, leaving a £5.7m reserve at 31 March 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Broxtowe Borough Council underspent its General Fund revenue budget by £2.5m in 2025/26. That left a General Fund Reserve of £5.7m at 31 March 2026, according to the council's Medium Term Financial Strategy and Business Strategy, dated October 2026, which goes to Cabinet on 3 November.

The paper attributes the underspend to a mix of underspends, additional income, budget carry forwards, changes in provisions, government grants and financial management. It does not give a figure for each of these.

The 2025/26 outturn is the starting point for the reserve forecasts in the strategy. The £5.7m balance is the figure from which the council's projections for later years begin.
news_drafts.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL

news_drafts.headline: Broxtowe housing scheme delivered a year early as council addresses regulator concerns
news_drafts.lead: Broxtowe's Hemlock Gate housing scheme is completing in 2026/27, a year ahead of schedule, allowing the council to bring forward £1.838m in spending and start collecting rental income for its housing account sooner than expected. The acceleration comes as the developer prioritises the council's social housing units during a slowdown in the housing market. Meanwhile, the council is responding to a C3 judgment from the Regulator of Social Housing following an October inspection by implementing a refreshed improvement plan and restructuring its housing teams to centralise compliance, with changes to take effect in October 2026. The council is also managing immediate pressures on its capital programme, including an additional £120,000 of borrowing needed to upgrade lifeline alarm systems in its Independent Living schemes before the analogue phone line switch-off on 31 January 2027, and a 53 per cent cost increase in council office repairs due to scaffolding price inflation. The section 151 officer, the council's chief finance officer, has flagged potential future cost pressures on the housing account, though none have materialised yet.

findings.headline: Bed and breakfast accommodation was used for 257 nights in Q2 2026/27, against a Q2 figure of 350 nights.
findings.detail: The paper reports 15 households in bed and breakfast accommodation during Q2 2026/27, and notes the council has 22 units for temporary accommodation. The indicator is rated green.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are a growing demand pressure for councils, and a finance officer will want to see how the B&B nights compare with the annual target.
findings.figures: 257 days; 15 households; 350 (Q2); 1,400 annual target; 546 in the prior year column
findings.quote: During Q2 2026/27, 15 different Households were in bed and breakfast accommodation for a total of 257 days.

findings.headline: Sundry debtors collected in-year were 73% at Q2 against a 90% target, with the paper expecting the year-end position to meet target.
findings.detail: The paper says performance on this indicator depends heavily on when invoices are raised and on the statutory payment period, and that instalment arrangements are expected to bring the year-end position to target.
findings.matters: Slow sundry debt collection ties up council cash and can require bad debt provision, and a finance officer will check the year-end recovery the paper expects.
findings.quote: It is expected that the year-end position will meet the target as instalment arrangements

findings.headline: Council Tax collected in-year was 55.5% at Q2 against a 55.0% target, and Business Rates 57.6% against 55.0%.
findings.detail: The paper states that collection rates for both Council Tax and Non-domestic Rates continue to be above target at Q2.
findings.matters: Council Tax and Business Rates collection drive the council's cash position, and a finance director would compare them with the same quarter last year.
findings.quote: Collection rates continue to be above target.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit overpayment recovery stands at 6.3% against a Q2 target of 8%, and the paper ties this to the move to Universal Credit.
findings.detail: The paper says the method of recovering Housing Benefit overpayments has changed since Universal Credit was introduced. With fewer opportunities to recover the debt directly, the rate of recovery has fallen, and the indicator is now recorded as data only.
findings.matters: Falling recovery of legacy Housing Benefit overpayments is a receivable loss that councils with the same legacy caseload will be watching.
findings.quote: With the Council having less opportunity to recover the debt directly, it has significantly impacted on the rate of recovery.

findings.headline: The council's spend under its successor to Discretionary Housing Payments is £158,459, against a DWP contribution of £99,168
findings.detail: The scheme has changed from Discretionary Housing Payments to the Crisis Resilience Fund under a policy approved by Cabinet on 21 July 2026. The paper says the council is expected to fund in excess of 100% of the DWP grant in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council spending more than the grant it receives on a hardship scheme is paying the difference from its own resources, which finance directors will track against budget.
findings.figures: £99,168; £158,459; 103% DHP contribution against DWP grant in the indicator table; in excess of 100%
findings.quote: The DWP contribution is currently £99,168 for the year but the Council has contributed a further figure allowing for a total spend of £158,459.
